title: VNet & Subnet Architecture
summary: A three-tier VNet with NSG-protected subnets, Azure Bastion, a VPN gateway and NAT Gateway for outbound traffic.

nodes.label: Internet
nodes.detail: Inbound internet traffic reaches only resources with public IPs or behind a public load balancer/gateway, and only if NSGs allow it.

nodes.label: Web VMs
nodes.detail: The web subnet's NSG allows HTTPS from the Internet and denies everything else inbound (default DenyAllInBound).

nodes.label: App VMs
nodes.detail: Only the web tier can reach the app tier, e.g., an NSG rule allowing the Web ASG on port 8080.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.detail: The data tier is reachable only from the app tier on the database port.

nodes.label: Azure Bastion
nodes.detail: Admins connect through the portal over 443; VMs need no public IPs and management ports aren't exposed.

nodes.label: VPN gateway
nodes.detail: Gateways must be deployed in the subnet named GatewaySubnet. Don't put other resources (or an NSG) there.

nodes.label: NAT gateway
nodes.detail: Associated with the app subnet to give outbound internet access through fixed Standard public IPs. Outbound only.

nodes.label: Admin
nodes.detail: Uses the Azure portal to start a Bastion session.

nodes.label: On-prem
nodes.detail: Its address space must not overlap 10.0.0.0/16.

steps.title: Address space and subnets
steps.text: The VNet is carved into subnets per tier. Each subnet loses 5 addresses to Azure.

steps.title: Tier-to-tier rules
steps.text: NSGs allow only the next tier in, on the right port — classic segmentation.

steps.title: Secure management
steps.text: Bastion in AzureBastionSubnet gives RDP/SSH without public IPs on VMs.

steps.title: Hybrid and outbound
steps.text: A VPN gateway in GatewaySubnet connects on-premises; NAT Gateway gives the app tier outbound internet via fixed IPs.

examExpects: Special subnets have exact names and minimum sizes: GatewaySubnet, AzureBastionSubnet (/26+), AzureFirewallSubnet (/26).
Subnets in a VNet can communicate by default; segment with NSGs/ASGs.
Calculate usable IPs: subnet size minus 5.
Avoid public IPs on VMs: use Bastion for management and load balancers/gateways for app traffic.

title: VNet Peering & Gateway Transit (Hub and Spoke)
summary: Peered spokes reach on-premises through the hub's gateway, but peering isn't transitive between spokes.

nodes.label: On-premises
nodes.detail: Connected to the hub with a site-to-site VPN or ExpressRoute.

nodes.label: VPN gateway
nodes.detail: The hub peering links enable 'Allow gateway transit' so spokes can use this gateway.

nodes.label: Azure Firewall
nodes.detail: To route spoke-to-spoke through the hub, add UDRs pointing to the firewall and enable 'Allow forwarded traffic'.

nodes.label: App VMs
nodes.detail: Spoke peering link enables 'Use remote gateways' — the spoke must not have its own gateway.

nodes.label: App VMs
nodes.detail: Peered with the hub only.

steps.title: Hub and spokes
steps.text: Spokes peer with a hub that holds shared services: gateway and firewall.

steps.title: Gateway transit
steps.text: Allow gateway transit (hub) + Use remote gateways (spoke) lets Spoke 1 reach on-premises through the hub's VPN gateway.

steps.title: Not transitive
steps.text: Spoke 1 can't reach Spoke 2 just because both peer with the hub.

steps.title: Fix spoke-to-spoke
steps.text: Either peer the spokes directly or route through the firewall with UDRs and allow forwarded traffic.

examExpects: Peering requires non-overlapping address spaces and is non-transitive.
Gateway transit settings: hub = Allow gateway transit; spoke = Use remote gateways.
Spoke-to-spoke needs direct peering or hub routing (NVA/Firewall + UDR).
Global peering connects VNets across regions over the Microsoft backbone.

title: NSG Rule Processing
summary: Inbound traffic is checked by the subnet NSG and then the NIC NSG; within each, the lowest priority number that matches wins.

nodes.label: Inbound packet
nodes.detail: A 5-tuple: source IP/port, destination IP/port and protocol.

nodes.label: Subnet NSG
nodes.detail: Rule 100 matches first, so the subnet NSG allows the packet and evaluation moves to the NIC NSG.

nodes.label: NIC NSG
nodes.detail: No custom rule matches Internet traffic, so default rule 65500 denies it. Both NSGs must allow traffic.

nodes.label: VM
nodes.detail: Fix: add an allow rule for 443 from Internet (or the needed source) on the NIC NSG, or remove the NIC NSG.

nodes.label: 100 · Allow 443
nodes.detail: Lowest number = highest priority. First match wins and evaluation stops.

nodes.label: 4000 · Deny any
nodes.detail: Never evaluated for this packet because rule 100 already matched.

nodes.label: 65500 · DenyAllInBound
nodes.detail: Default rules can't be deleted, only overridden by lower-numbered rules.

nodes.label: 110 · Allow 443
nodes.detail: Only allows traffic from the VirtualNetwork service tag, so an Internet source doesn't match.

nodes.label: 65000 · AllowVnetInBound
nodes.detail: Allows traffic from the VNet and connected networks — not the Internet.

nodes.label: 65500 · DenyAllInBound
nodes.detail: This catch-all matches, so the NIC NSG denies the packet.

steps.title: Subnet NSG first (inbound)
steps.text: Rules are checked by priority. Rule 100 matches HTTPS from Internet → allowed.

steps.title: First match wins
steps.text: Rule 4000 and the defaults are never reached for this packet.

steps.title: Then the NIC NSG
steps.text: Rule 110 only allows VirtualNetwork sources; AllowVnetInBound doesn't match Internet either.

steps.title: Default deny
steps.text: 65500 DenyAllInBound matches, so the packet is dropped. Outbound traffic is evaluated in the reverse order: NIC NSG first, then subnet NSG.

examExpects: Evaluate by priority (lowest first), not by list order; first match wins.
Inbound: subnet NSG → NIC NSG. Outbound: NIC NSG → subnet NSG. Both must allow.
Know the default rules and that NSGs are stateful.
Use IP flow verify / NSG diagnostics to identify the rule that blocks a flow.

title: Private Endpoint vs Service Endpoint
summary: Service endpoints secure a service's public endpoint to your subnet; private endpoints bring the service into your VNet with a private IP.

nodes.label: VM in Subnet A
nodes.detail: The service endpoint is enabled on the subnet. Traffic takes an optimized backbone route and carries the subnet identity.

nodes.label: Storage firewall
nodes.detail: The service's network rules must allow the subnet. Both halves are required.

nodes.label: Storage account
nodes.detail: The account still resolves to a public IP. The endpoint applies to the whole service type from that subnet.

nodes.label: On-premises
nodes.detail: Service endpoints don't extend to on-premises networks; they'd have to use the public endpoint and IP rules.

nodes.label: VM in Subnet B
nodes.detail: Connects to mystorage.blob.core.windows.net, which DNS resolves to the private endpoint's IP.

nodes.label: Private endpoint
nodes.detail: A NIC in your subnet mapped to one specific resource and sub-resource (e.g., this account's blob service).

nodes.label: Storage account
nodes.detail: With private endpoints in place you can disable public network access entirely.

nodes.label: Private DNS zone
nodes.detail: privatelink.blob.core.windows.net linked to the VNet holds the A record pointing to 10.1.2.5.

nodes.label: On-premises
nodes.detail: On-premises clients reach the private IP over the hybrid connection, given DNS forwarding to resolve the privatelink zone.

steps.title: Service endpoint
steps.text: Enable it on the subnet, then allow the subnet in the storage firewall. The service keeps its public IP.

steps.title: Limitation
steps.text: On-premises clients can't use the service endpoint.

steps.title: Private endpoint
steps.text: A private IP in your VNet maps to the specific storage account; public access can be disabled.

steps.title: DNS makes it work
steps.text: The privatelink zone resolves the normal name to the private IP — including for on-premises clients via DNS forwarding.

examExpects: Private endpoint = private IP for one resource, reachable from peered and on-premises networks; public access can be disabled.
Service endpoint = subnet identity to the service's public endpoint; no private IP; not usable from on-premises.
Private endpoints need DNS integration (privatelink zones).
Service endpoints require configuration on both the subnet and the service firewall.

title: Azure Load Balancer Architecture
summary: Frontend IP, load-balancing rule, health probe and backend pool working together at Layer 4.

nodes.label: Clients
nodes.detail: Connect to the frontend IP; Load Balancer doesn't terminate connections — it forwards flows.

nodes.label: Frontend IP
nodes.detail: Public frontend for internet traffic, or a private IP from a subnet for an internal load balancer.

nodes.label: LB rule
nodes.detail: Maps frontend IP:port to backend pool:port, with a probe and session persistence setting.

nodes.label: Health probe
nodes.detail: Probes come from 168.63.129.16 (AzureLoadBalancer service tag). Instances that fail stop receiving new flows.

nodes.label: Backend pool
nodes.detail: Backends are NICs or IP addresses within a single virtual network.

nodes.label: VM 1
nodes.detail: Receives new flows.

nodes.label: VM 2
nodes.detail: Receives new flows.

nodes.label: VM 3
nodes.detail: Taken out of rotation until the probe succeeds again. Check the app, the probe path and NSGs.

steps.title: Frontend
steps.text: Clients connect to the frontend IP (public or internal).

steps.title: Rule
steps.text: The load-balancing rule maps the frontend port to the backend pool port using a 5-tuple hash by default.

steps.title: Health probe
steps.text: Probes decide which instances are eligible.

steps.title: Distribution
steps.text: New flows go only to healthy VMs 1 and 2.

examExpects: Layer 4 only: TCP/UDP, no URL routing or TLS termination.
Troubleshoot 'no traffic' via health probe configuration and NSG rules (allow AzureLoadBalancer).
Public vs internal frontends; Standard SKU is secure by default.
Session persistence options: None (5-tuple), Client IP, Client IP and protocol.

title: Application Gateway Architecture
summary: Layer 7 routing: listener → WAF → path-based rule → backend pools, with TLS termination.

nodes.label: Browsers
nodes.detail: Clients connect over HTTPS to the gateway's frontend IP.

nodes.label: Listener
nodes.detail: A multi-site listener matches host name contoso.com. TLS terminates here using the certificate (optionally from Key Vault).

nodes.label: WAF policy
nodes.detail: Inspects requests for attacks such as SQL injection and XSS; Detection or Prevention mode.

nodes.label: Path-based rule
nodes.detail: Matches the URL path to choose a backend pool and backend settings.

nodes.label: Health probes
nodes.detail: Unhealthy servers are removed from rotation.

nodes.label: Images pool
nodes.detail: Backend pool for static content servers.

nodes.label: API pool
nodes.detail: Backend pool for API servers; could be App Service or VMSS.

nodes.label: Default pool
nodes.detail: Requests that match no path rule go to the default backend.

steps.title: Listener
steps.text: The listener accepts HTTPS for contoso.com and terminates TLS.

steps.title: WAF
steps.text: Requests are inspected for common web attacks.

steps.title: Path-based routing
steps.text: /images/* and /api/* go to different pools; everything else goes to the default pool.

steps.title: Health
steps.text: Probes keep only healthy servers in each pool.

examExpects: Path-based routing, multi-site hosting, TLS termination and WAF are Application Gateway features.
It's regional and lives in its own dedicated subnet.
Know components: frontend IP, listener, rule, backend settings, backend pool, probe.
For global HTTP load balancing, consider Front Door.

title: Hybrid Connectivity: VPN Gateway & ExpressRoute
summary: Site-to-site and point-to-site VPN over the internet versus a private ExpressRoute circuit.

nodes.label: VPN device
nodes.detail: Your on-premises VPN appliance; its public IP goes in the local network gateway.

nodes.label: Servers
nodes.detail: On-premises address ranges are listed in the local network gateway (or learned via BGP).

nodes.label: Local network gateway
nodes.detail: An Azure resource that represents your on-premises site. The connection resource links it to the VPN gateway with a shared key.

nodes.label: VPN gateway
nodes.detail: Terminates IPsec/IKE tunnels and P2S connections. Route-based is required for P2S and ExpressRoute coexistence.

nodes.label: ExpressRoute gateway
nodes.detail: Connects the VNet to an ExpressRoute circuit's private peering.

nodes.label: Workload VMs
nodes.detail: Reachable from on-premises over either path.

nodes.label: Connectivity provider
nodes.detail: A private connection via a provider — not over the internet, and not encrypted by default.

nodes.label: Remote laptop
nodes.detail: Individual clients connect with point-to-site, authenticating with certificates, Entra ID or RADIUS.

steps.title: Site-to-site VPN
steps.text: An IPsec tunnel over the internet between the on-premises device and the Azure VPN gateway.

steps.title: Configuration objects
steps.text: The local network gateway describes on-premises (public IP + prefixes); a connection with a shared key links it to the VPN gateway.

steps.title: Point-to-site
steps.text: Individual devices connect directly to the VPN gateway.

steps.title: ExpressRoute
steps.text: A private circuit through a provider reaches the ExpressRoute gateway — no internet path. Often paired with S2S VPN as failover.

examExpects: Local network gateway = on-premises public IP and address prefixes.
S2S for sites, P2S for individual clients; route-based VPN for most scenarios.
ExpressRoute is private (not internet) and not encrypted by default.
Both gateway types live in GatewaySubnet; gateway creation takes a long time.

title: DNS Resolution in Azure
summary: How a VM resolves names through Azure-provided DNS, private DNS zones and public DNS — and how on-premises joins in.

nodes.label: VM in VNet
nodes.detail: By default the VNet uses Azure-provided DNS, so the VM sends its query to 168.63.129.16.

nodes.label: Azure DNS
nodes.detail: Azure's resolver answers from private zones linked to the VNet first, then Azure-internal names, then public DNS.

nodes.label: Private DNS zone
nodes.detail: Linked to the VNet. Holds an A record for mystore → 10.0.2.5 (the private endpoint).

nodes.label: Answer: 10.0.2.5
nodes.detail: The VM connects to the private IP — traffic never uses the public endpoint.

nodes.label: Public DNS
nodes.detail: Names not found in linked private zones are resolved recursively from public DNS (e.g., Azure DNS public zones).

nodes.label: On-prem client
nodes.detail: On-premises can't query 168.63.129.16 directly. Configure a conditional forwarder for the privatelink zone.

nodes.label: DNS Private Resolver
nodes.detail: Gives on-premises DNS a private IP in the VNet to forward to; it resolves using Azure DNS and linked private zones.

steps.title: Query
steps.text: The VM asks Azure-provided DNS at 168.63.129.16.

steps.title: Private zone lookup
steps.text: Because the privatelink zone is linked to the VNet, Azure DNS answers from it.

steps.title: Fallback
steps.text: Names not in linked zones resolve via public DNS.

steps.title: On-premises
steps.text: On-premises DNS forwards Azure zones to the Private Resolver's inbound endpoint.

examExpects: Private DNS zones resolve only for linked VNets; auto-registration creates VM records automatically.
Private endpoints depend on privatelink zones resolving to the private IP.
Custom DNS servers must forward to 168.63.129.16 to use Azure private zones.
Public zones need NS delegation at the registrar.
